verses.1:
Al-Mizan introduces this Meccan sūrah as a general warning: after signs of God’s oneness, it promulgates a sharīʿah for the Prophet, warns that obedience and rejection bear their own consequences, and ends with recompense at the Resurrection. It finds no evidence for treating (45:14) as an exception to its Meccan character. The Book is simply sent down from the All-mighty, All-wise God; grammatically, tanzīl al-kitāb is a verbal-noun construction whose sense is passive.

The heavens and earth are themselves signs, not merely containers for signs. Saying that signs are “in” them draws attention to their many jihāt wujūdihī, each a sign, whereas considering the thing as a whole makes it one sign. Their essential need (ḥājah dhātiyyah) for origination, their ordered and interconnected composition, and their subsumption under one cosmic order prove one Creator and governing Lord without a partner; reading “in the heavens” as “in the creation of the heavens” is needlessly strained. Human and animal creation likewise point to God: the human being unites a material body that returns to dust with a transcendent, immaterial spirit that survives death and is kept with God, while animals have living, sensing souls of a lower degree.

The alternation of night and day, rain as rizq, and the disposal of winds display a terrestrial order that provides for life and subtly alludes to resurrection. Al-Mizan distinguishes the straightforward signs of heaven and earth for believers, the signs in human and animal souls for those with certainty, and the varied, far-reaching signs of time, rain, and winds for those who apply reason. Certainty and reason proceed through ongoing reflection, unlike the already established basis of belief. It rejects accounts of the ordering of these three groups that either make reason subsequent to certainty, fail to explain why particular qualities accompany particular signs, or collapse certainty into mere knowledge and leave reason only speculative knowledge, which is inadmissible in belief.

Belief (īmān) is knowledge joined to practical adherence. Cosmic signs point to God’s unique creation, perfection, and freedom from need; Qur’anic signs point to those cosmic signs, doctrine, law, and approved moral qualities; miracles may be cosmic or non-cosmic signs. “These are the signs … recited” primarily means the Qur’anic signs, though it may unite them with the cosmic signs just mentioned. Al-Mizan prefers the reading that asks what discourse people could believe after these Qur’anic signs, rather than the reading that contrasts God’s speech with His signs.

The sinful liar is an addict to lying (affāk) who hears Qur’anic signs yet persists (iṣrār) arrogantly in unbelief as though he had not heard. On learning any sign, he derides the signs themselves, displaying utter ignorance; the resulting punishment is humiliating precisely in response to arrogance and derision. Hell is a foreordained destiny “behind” such people although they are heading toward it; neither wealth, rank, supporters, nor the idols or alleged intercessory guardians they took besides God will help them. The repeated threats are painful, humiliating, and great. The Qur’an is guidance in the emphatic sense, and rejecting its signs after mocking it brings punishment of defilement, the severest punishment, whose original sense is confusion.

The address then turns to all people through manifest signs of lordship. God disposed the sea for human benefit, enabling ships to sail by His creative command, kun; the properties of things, like the things themselves, are attributed to Him. Sailing enables people to seek His grace, meaning sustenance, and should elicit thanks. His disposing everything in heaven and earth means that the visible world operates as one natural order that links its parts and human beings, permitting ever wider benefit. Everything originates from Him—its essences, properties, and their interconnection—without prior precedent; rival readings of “from Him” are rejected as strained. This origin and ordered subjection are signs for reflection (tafakkur).

verses.3: Al-Mizan holds that the heavens and earth are themselves God’s signs, not merely places containing signs. Expressions that say a sign is “in” a thing direct attention to its multiple jihāt wujūdihī, each of which is a sign; viewed as one whole, the thing is only one sign. Their essential need (ḥājah dhātiyyah) for an originator, their remarkable composition and interconnection, and their unified cosmic order show that they have one Creator and governing Lord without a partner; otherwise their arrangement would be contradictory and conflict-ridden. The proposed implicit construction “in the creation of the heavens” is therefore an unnecessarily strained reading.
verses.4: Al-Mizan reads bathth, God’s “scattering” of animals, as creating, separating, and spreading them through the world. Human creation and animal creation are signs for people on the path of certainty. The human being is not only a terrestrial material body that decomposes after death, but also has a transcendent, immaterial spirit that survives death and is kept with God; animal souls are living and sensing, though lower than human souls. Contemplating these created realities discloses God’s oneness in lordship and divinity, without a partner.
verses.5:
Al-Mizan treats the alternation of night and day, their changing lengths with the seasons, as part of the natural order by which God arranges sustenance and educates earthly inhabitants. “Provision” (rizq) sent down from heaven is rain, either figuratively named for the provision it causes or itself a provision; “heaven” here can mean the sky or clouds. Reviving the earth means bringing forth its plants and subtly alludes to the Resurrection. The disposal of winds is their changing direction and includes benefits such as moving clouds, pollinating plants, and clearing harmful air.

These signs belong to people who apply reason: those who use God-given intellect to distinguish truth from falsehood and right from wrong. Al-Mizan distinguishes them from the signs of heaven and earth for believers and the signs in humans and animals for people with certainty. The first give simple guidance to every level of believer that the world is neither self-originating nor chance-made, so its Creator is Lord of all. Living and sensing souls belong, in their higher aspect, to the realm of dominion (malakūt), apprehended by people of certainty. The complex, varied, terrestrial benefits of night and day, rain, and winds require deeper, meticulous contemplation, so only those who apply reason benefit from them in this distinctive way.

The wording also matters: believers are called muʾminīn because this basic belief is already fixed in them, while qawmun yūqinūn and qawmun yaʿqilūn use imperfect verbs for the ongoing, stage-by-stage work of certainty and reasoning. Al-Mizan rejects an account that makes the sequence belief, certainty, and reason ascending stages, because its own definition of reason would require reason before certainty, which cannot admit doubt. It also rejects explanations that order the signs by causal or final-causal dependence: they do not explain why faith, certainty, and reason are respectively attached to the three sets, and create further reversals. An account that says the groups mean, respectively, believers, seekers of certainty, and people with neither is likewise inadequate: it explains the qualities but not the signs, wrongly restricts each set to one quality, and reduces certainty to knowledge while leaving reason only speculative knowledge (ʿilm ẓannī), which is inadmissible in belief.
verses.6:
Al-Mizan defines īmān as knowing something and adhering to it in practice; knowledge without adherence is not belief. Cosmic āyāt are realities whose existence points to God as the sole Creator, perfect and free from need, so believing in them entails believing what they indicate about Him. Qur’anic āyāt point to cosmic signs, doctrine, practical laws, and divinely approved moral qualities; believing them likewise entails belief in what they indicate. Miracles may be cosmic signs or non-cosmic signs, as with the Qur’an’s inimitability.

“These are the signs of God that We recite” primarily identifies the Qur’anic signs recited to the hearer, though it may also unite those signs with the cosmic signs just discussed. Al-Mizan prefers the interpretation of “what discourse will they believe after God and His signs?” as: if they will not believe this Qur’anic discourse and its signs, what other discourse could they believe? It rejects the alternative that makes “discourse” God’s speech and “signs” cosmic signs as less fitting, despite Ṭabrisī’s reported distinction between Qur’anic discourse that separates ḥaqq from bāṭil and its signs as proofs separating ṣaḥīḥ from fāsid.
verses.7: Al-Mizan reads “woe” as “perish,” and affāk as the intensive form for one addicted to lying; athīm is one who commits sins. The sinful liar hears the Qur’an’s signs but then persists (iṣrār)—keeps rather than abandons unbelief—in arrogant refusal to humble himself before truth, as though he had not heard. Thumma marks a sequence in rank, not time, and conveys distance. The promised painful punishment is for this persistent, disdainful response.
verses.8: Al-Mizan reads “woe” as “perish,” and affāk as the intensive form for one addicted to lying; athīm is one who commits sins. The sinful liar hears the Qur’an’s signs but then persists (iṣrār)—keeps rather than abandons unbelief—in arrogant refusal to humble himself before truth, as though he had not heard. Thumma marks a sequence in rank, not time, and conveys distance. The promised painful punishment is for this persistent, disdainful response.
verses.9: Al-Mizan takes “them” to mean the signs themselves. Linking derision directly to the signs, rather than merely to what the sinner learned about them, emphasizes his utter ignorance: the persistent sinful liar derides every sign when he learns anything of it. The humiliating punishment means abasement and disgrace, aptly answering his arrogance and mockery, and ulāʾika includes every such sinful liar.
verses.10: Al-Mizan explains that Hell is said to be “behind” people absorbed in this world because they ignore the consequences of turning from truth, though they are actually proceeding toward it. Warāʾ can mean what lies in front as well as behind; here Hell is in any case a foreordained decree. What they have earned is their worldly wealth and its like, and the indefinite “anything” belittles it: neither wealth, rank, nor supporters will help them at all on the Day of Judgment. Their guardians besides God are either the idol-deities they regarded as lords and expected to intercede, or the idols themselves. The great punishment reiterates the preceding threats, variously called painful, humiliating, and great.
verses.11: Al-Mizan identifies “this” with the Qur’an and calls it guidance by hyperbole, as one might say “Zayd is justice.” Defilement is the severest kind of punishment and originally means confusion. In the setting of the faithless deriding and mocking the Qur’an, the verse warns those who reject its signs.
verses.12: Al-Mizan says that, after warning the disdainful mockers, the discourse turns to all people through undeniable signs of God’s lordship. God disposed the sea “for you,” primarily for human benefit, so ships can float and travel; it is also possible that the phrase denotes people’s taming of the sea by God’s leave. Ships sail by His command because sailing, like every property of things, is created through His creative command, kun. Riding ships enables people to seek His grace, meaning sustenance, and the blessing of the subdued sea calls for thanks.
verses.13:
Al-Mizan reads this as a more general statement following the particular example of the sea. “All” stresses the inclusion of everything in heaven and earth, and “for you” has the same force as in the preceding verse. Their subjection means that the visible world’s parts operate under a single natural order that connects them with one another and with human beings, enabling human benefit, including civilization’s continuing discovery of further uses.

“From Him” means originating with God: He creates the essences of things without precedent, their properties, and their interconnection in this natural order. Alternative readings of “from Him” are rejected as tortuous. This total originating subjection is therefore a sign for people who reflect (tafakkur).
verses.14:
Al-Mizan reads the command, revealed in Mecca, as directing the Prophet to tell believers to forgive the faithless who insulted them, belittled the Prophet, and mocked God’s signs. The construction replaces the imperative ighfirū with yaghfirū, as in (14:31), but its force is still the command to forgive. Here forgiveness means excusing and ignoring them rather than arguing with them; believers need not confront people against whom punishment has already been decreed, because their deeds will fully overtake them.

Those who do not expect God’s days deny days on which He judges and exercises authority, including death, barzakh, the Resurrection, and worldly destruction. “That He may requite a people” supplies the rationale: the Day of Recompense is one of those days, and God Himself will repay their earned deeds. The indefinite, unqualified “a people” instead of “them” belittles these deniers and conveys that God has no concern for them. Al-Mizan therefore takes the verse to connect directly to the preceding threats and rejects the alternative explanations as unfounded.
verses.15: Al-Mizan takes this as explaining why God will requite the people just mentioned, which accounts for the absence of a new connective. Deeds do not vanish: righteous action benefits its doer, evil harms its doer, and all return to their Lord to be repaid good for good and evil for evil.
verses.16:
Al-Mizan presents Israel’s reception of the Book, judgment, prophethood, good provision, favor, and manifest signs as showing that the Prophet’s sharīʿah is not unprecedented: guiding servants to their good and happiness is God’s responsibility. The Book most likely means the Torah, not Scripture generally. The Evangel introduced no new divine code but followed the Torah’s, and David’s Psalms are supplications and invocations; the general reading is unlikely because the Qur’an calls kitāb a scripture containing a sharīʿah. Judgment is the Book’s rulings and edicts which people must enact, and prophethood was abundantly granted among the Israelites.

The good provision is manna and quails. Favor over “the nations” may mean particular advantages, such as many prophets and miracles, over all peoples, or complete favor over the peoples of their own time.
verses.17: Al-Mizan defines the manifest signs as signs that remove doubt and hesitation from truth. It reports a reading of amr as the matter of the Prophet, namely clear indications of his truthfulness found in the Israelites’ books. Their later religious disagreement and the admixture of falsehood with truth did not arise from ignorance or doubt after knowledge had come, but from reciprocal spite among their scholars. These disagreements will not be forgotten: God will judge and recompense them on the Day of Resurrection according to their conduct.
verses.18: Al-Mizan says the direct address is also for the Prophet’s community. Sharīʿah, literally a path leading down to water, is the specific path of the matter of religion: Islam, bestowed on the Prophet and his community. He is commanded to follow revealed religion and not the desires of the ignorant that oppose it. This shows both that the Prophet himself was bound to follow the religion and that every practical rule not based on, or traceable to, revelation is an ignorant desire without sound knowledge.
verses.19: Al-Mizan explains that only God can meet the Prophet’s essential needs, and His religion—not the desires of the ignorant—is the way to do so; those people can avail him nothing against God. Wrongdoers are those who follow wayward desire, while the Godwary follow God’s religion. The former are guardians only of one another, whereas God is the guardian of those who follow His religion. One must therefore follow God’s religion to have Him as guardian, rather than follow their desires and receive no help. Calling followers of another religion wrongdoers accords with (7:44–45).
verses.20:
Al-Mizan identifies “this” with Islam’s clear path, or with the Qur’an as containing its practical duties. Baṣāʾir are perceptions corresponding to reality and, here, the means of perceiving: every law and rule of the Religion enables people to see and follow the path of God and happiness. It is insights for all people, but guidance and mercy for people who have certainty (īqān) about God’s signs and the foundational doctrines (uṣūl al-maʿārif).

The restriction shows that hudā is not mere correct perception but arrival at one’s destination, and that raḥmah is the mercy reserved for the Godwary believers in the Messenger. Divine mercy has degrees corresponding to degrees of faith. In its broadest sense it is all good emanating from God, so the Qur’an’s sharīʿah, and the Prophet who brings it, are mercy for everyone.
verses.21:
Al-Mizan treats the rhetorical question as rejecting the idea that those who earn misdeeds will be treated like believers who do righteous deeds, equal in life and death. Ijtirāḥ means earning, derived from wounding because an act has an effect, and a sayyiʾah harms its doer by inviting rebuke. The grammatical details support reading the two groups as the subject of their equality, but the contextual conclusion is that this judgment is evil and hence false.

They are unequal in life because believers act upon a true perception of their condition and receive guidance and mercy, while the evildoer has the opposite condition. They are unequal in death because death is neither annihilation nor the soul’s end, but return to God and transition to the eternal Hereafter: the righteous believer has happiness and ease there, while others have misery and suffering. Al-Mizan holds this contextual reading to be superior to the numerous disputed alternatives.
verses.22:
Al-Mizan takes the heavens and earth to mean the whole perceptible universe (al-ʿālam al-mashhūd). Their creation “with truth” means it is neither vain nor purposeless, but ordered toward a subsistent, lasting world beyond this realm of generation and corruption. Requiting every soul for what it earned is just recompense: obedience receives reward, sin punishment, and no one is wronged.

The verse thus gives two arguments for the Resurrection. Truth in creation requires the enduring world beyond this one, while justice requires that every soul receive what it deserves; since that full recompense is not realized here, it must occur there. This refutes the claim that evildoer and good-doer are equal in death, and consequently in life: promised recompense requires obedience in this world, where the good-doer acts with insight, fulfills moral duty, and prepares for tomorrow, unlike the evildoer in blindness and error.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan reads “Have you seen?” as an expression of astonishment. The placement of “god” before “desire” shows a person who knows he has a real God to worship but substitutes his own desire and obeys it. Obedience is worship because it displays the servant’s total submission; therefore whoever obeys desire has made it a god, though obedience belongs only to God or to one whose obedience God commands.

God’s leading such a person astray “upon knowledge” is recompense for knowingly following desire. Knowledge is not guidance, nor error ignorance: guidance requires knowing and acting upon what one knows, whereas knowledge without action through desire leads to error. Al-Mizan rejects the reading that “knowledge” is merely God’s knowledge of the person’s state as unsuitable to the context. The seal on hearing and heart and blindfold on sight explain this misguidance: through arrogance and desire, he neither receives nor understands truth or perceives it in God’s signs, despite possessing knowledge. Since no guide exists except God, no one can guide the person after Him; the verse calls readers to take warning that guidance cannot be attained while following desire.
verses.24:
Al-Mizan identifies this as the idolaters’ denial of the Resurrection, not the doctrine of the philosophical Dahriyyah, who held the world eternally beginningless and endless. Dahr originally denotes the world’s duration from beginning to end and then any long period, unlike zamān, which covers long and short periods. Their claim that life is only this worldly life means there is no Hereafter: older generations die, new generations live, and time continuously ages, ruins, and destroys living things. Thus death is not a passage to another abode or a return to God.

Perhaps this was a belief of some ignorant Arab idolaters. Al-Mizan notes that the common idolatrous doctrine was reincarnation (tanāsukh), under which imperfect souls enter new bodies for happiness or misery as recompense; it reports the resulting interpretation of the verse but finds it inconsistent with “nothing but age destroys us” and with their later demand that their forefathers be brought back, which assumes they have ceased to exist. Other readings are set aside. Their denial is conjecture without knowledge or proof, while ample evidence affirms the Resurrection.
verses.25: Al-Mizan says the manifest signs contain proofs that affirm the Resurrection and leave no doubt. The deniers’ demand, “Bring our fathers back,” is called an argument only ironically: after proof has been made clear, they make the senseless, mocking demand for proof of its possibility by resurrecting their forefathers. It demonstrates that their denial of a life beyond this world rests on no knowledge.
verses.26:
Al-Mizan says that although the demand to resurrect their fathers deserves no answer, God commands the Prophet to affirm the possibility (imkān) of resurrection. The God who first gives life, causes death, and possesses the dominion of heaven and earth can gather people on the certain Day of Resurrection, judge them, and recompense them as He wills.

When the Hour “sets in,” everything belonging to it—Resurrection, accounting, recompense, and its manifestation—comes to pass; “on that day” reinforces this. The falsifiers are those who declared truth false and turned away from it. Their loss (khasr) is not chiefly worldly or commercial loss, but loss of personal acquisitions such as health, vigor, sense, faith, and divine reward; Qur’anic loss always has this sense. Ibṭāl can mean to nullify or to speak what has no truth, so the falsifiers are the ones who treated truth as false, and they will be losers on the day of return to God.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan says that although the demand to resurrect their fathers deserves no answer, God commands the Prophet to affirm the possibility (imkān) of resurrection. The God who first gives life, causes death, and possesses the dominion of heaven and earth can gather people on the certain Day of Resurrection, judge them, and recompense them as He wills.

When the Hour “sets in,” everything belonging to it—Resurrection, accounting, recompense, and its manifestation—comes to pass; “on that day” reinforces this. The falsifiers are those who declared truth false and turned away from it. Their loss (khasr) is not chiefly worldly or commercial loss, but loss of personal acquisitions such as health, vigor, sense, faith, and divine reward; Qur’anic loss always has this sense. Ibṭāl can mean to nullify or to speak what has no truth, so the falsifiers are the ones who treated truth as false, and they will be losers on the day of return to God.
verses.28: Al-Mizan explains jathuw as sinking to one’s knees. The address, though directed to the Prophet, is general: every nation will be seen kneeling in fear and humiliation and summoned to its book, its complete record of deeds, to be requited for what it did. The verse also indicates that each nation has its own book, just as each individual has one.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan distinguishes transcription, nastansikh, from ordinary writing. Naskh may mean effacing one thing with what follows it, but in copying a book it transfers a text’s form to another material without erasing the first; istinsākh is undertaking that copying. Since the object copied is normally its source, “what you used to do” cannot simply mean external deeds being written down. It means deeds as they exist in the Guarded Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), from which they are transcribed. A person’s record is therefore both a record of deeds and a part of the Guarded Tablet; the angels’ recording correlates their transcription with the deeds performed. Al-Mizan attributes this explanation to Shiʿi narrations from Imam al-Ṣādiq and Sunni narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās.

Accordingly, “This is Our book” is God’s speech to the people gathered at the Resurrection, not the angels’ speech. It refers, according to context, to the record of deeds and thereby to the Guarded Tablet, called a book both because it is written by God’s command and to honor it. It speaks truly by testifying to and displaying their deeds so unmistakably that denial is impossible. Al-Mizan rejects as highly improbable the alternatives that make it the angels’ speech or reduce transcription to generic writing, including the version that identifies the book with the Guarded Tablet while giving transcription that generic sense.
verses.30: Al-Mizan turns here to the two outcomes on that day: believers who do righteous deeds are the felicitous and rewarded, while arrogant, faithless sinners are wretched and punished. God’s mercy is the divine effusion that grants felicity to those admitted into it, and Paradise is part of it. This is the manifest, unmistakable victory.
verses.31: Al-Mizan says the faithless are shrouded in unbelief through their own denial and obstinacy. The connective in the rebuke means that, as a consequence of their being faithless, they will be told that God’s signs—the revealed and preached divine proofs—were recited and made clear to them. Yet they arrogantly rejected them and became a guilty people, consumed by wrongdoing and sin.
verses.32: Al-Mizan takes God’s “promise” to mean the promised Resurrection and judgment conveyed by His messengers, with the certainty of the Hour explaining it; it may also mean that God promises truth. The deniers’ claim not to know what the Hour is does not express lack of intelligence, but contemptuously treats it as incomprehensible. Their statement that they have only conjecture and no certainty answers the manifest signs recited to them and displays their outrageous disdain for truth.
verses.33: Al-Mizan allows the Arabic to mean either the evils that they did or the evils of all that they did. Their evil deeds, or the evil inherent in them, will become manifest; this supports the view that deeds take on a physical reality for their doers. It also reports the reading that what appears is the recompense for those evils. What they used to deride is the punishment about which prophets and messengers warned them in this world, now surrounding them.
verses.34: Al-Mizan explains God’s “forgetting” as turning away from and abandoning them amid the terror and hardship of the Resurrection. It answers their having “forgotten” the encounter of that day by turning from God’s remembrance in this world and failing to prepare for it. The Fire is then their abode, without helpers.
verses.35: Al-Mizan says that the punishment already described follows because they mocked God’s signs and were deceived by worldly life, becoming so attached to it that they wished to remain in it forever. The address then turns from them to the Prophet: on that day they will remain in Hell forever and no propitiation or excuse will be accepted.
verses.36:
Al-Mizan reads this praise as the conclusion of the whole sūrah. God created and governs heaven, earth, and all things; creation has a purpose, returns to Him, and is recompensed. This requires divine paths toward happiness, the gathering at the Resurrection, and the just or merciful outcome due to every being. In all of this He governs and acts beautifully, so all praise belongs to Him.

The repeated “Lord of the heavens,” “Lord of the earth,” and then “Lord of the worlds” establishes the comprehensiveness of His lordship. Mentioning only worlds might invite the false thought that heaven or earth has another lord; mentioning only heaven and earth would not explicitly encompass everything else.
verses.37: Al-Mizan explains kibriyāʾ as the deepest greatness: magnificence beyond sense that returns to God’s infinitely perfect being (kamāl wujūdih). It includes the senses of being beyond submission, and of absolute authority, majesty, and superiority. His exclusive supremacy fills heaven and earth: nothing can be above or diminish Him. His being All-mighty means He overcomes all and is never overcome in creation and governance in this world or the Hereafter; His being All-wise means that both are founded on wisdom and beautiful conduct.
